content: Exercise therapy is regarded as a significant component in the management of arthritis. While its effectiveness has been extensively studied in adults with rheumatoid arthritis, there is limited research on its impact in children diagnosed with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effects of exercise therapy on functional ability, quality of life, and aerobic capacity in children with JIA. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PEDro, SportDiscus, Google Scholar, AMED, and others, covering studies published from January 1966 to October 2007. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) focusing on exercise therapy in JIA were selected for analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies and extracted the data. Out of 16 identified studies, only three met the inclusion criteria, involving a total of 212 participants. These studies adhered to at least seven out of ten methodological quality criteria. The data from these studies were pooled for meta-analysis, focusing on three primary outcomes: functional ability, quality of life, and aerobic capacity. The results showed the following: Functional ability (198 participants): Weighted mean difference (WMD) of -0.07 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.22 to 0.08). Quality of life (115 participants, measured using the CHQ-PhS): WMD of -3.96 (95% CI: -8.91 to 1.00). Aerobic capacity (124 participants): WMD of 0.04 (95% CI: -0.11 to 0.19). Although the results slightly favored exercise therapy, none of these outcomes reached statistical significance. Importantly, none of the studies reported any adverse effects associated with exercise therapy. The authors concluded that, based on silver-level evidence, there is no clinically meaningful or statistically significant proof that exercise therapy improves functional ability, quality of life, aerobic capacity, or pain in children with JIA. The limited number of available RCTs restricts the generalizability of these findings. However, both included and excluded studies consistently indicated that exercise therapy does not worsen arthritis or cause short-term harm. The review highlighted the substantial variability in outcome measures across studies, underscoring the need for standardized assessment tools or a core set of functional and physical outcome measures tailored for health research. This standardization is essential to generate robust evidence regarding the potential benefits of exercise therapy for JIA patients. While the short-term effects of exercise therapy appear promising, its long-term impact remains uncertain.
